newsitem.title: UK: Western engines needed for AN-124 cargo plane.
newsitem.headline: Western engines needed for AN-124 cargo plane.

text.p: Ukrainian-built engines on the giant Antonov 124 cargo plane are increasingly unreliable and need replacing by Western engines, Air Foyle chairman Chris Foyle said.
The UK-based company manages Antonov Design Bureau (ADB), which flies five 140-tonne capacity AN-124 aircraft, the world's largest commercially used freighter.
Foyle also told Reuters in an interview that the Ukraine/Russia-built AN 124's existing D18 engines are "becoming increasingly expensive to acquire, overhaul and maintain'.

"We are experiencing an AN-124 engine failure once every three or four months. The shelf life of the D18 is much shorter than that of a western counterpart and is more expensive to operate on a per hour basis," he said.
Foyle added that the plane's builder and operator, ADB, and Russia-based Volga-Dnepr, also a major operator of the AN-124, had been aware of the plane's engine limitations for at least five years.
"During that period, talks betwen ADB, Volga-Dnepr and Rolls-Royce, Pratt & Whitney and General Electric have taken place (about replacing the D18)," stated Foyle.
"The closest they got was to General Electric, which said it was prepared to finance an AN-124 engine development programme," he said.

"Maybe the answer could be for a Western engine financier to build and lease out the engines on a per hour basis. Otherwise, second-hand RB-211 or GE engines could be sought, but that would need huge investment in a recertification process," said Foyle.

However he added a massive amount of work and "tens of millions of dollars" would be needed to manufacture a suitable Western engine. This would involve development, 1,000 hours of flight testing and systems redesign.
In return, any manufacturer would want new engine orders.

But as there were only some 20 commercial and 30 military AN-124s in operation and requiring engine replacements, with no more in the production pipeline now or planned, this suggested scope for re-engining was limited.
